With Shopify International Selling, the problem of selling products internationally has been resolved. And today we are gonna understand how Shopify Markets work now, and how one store can provide multiple localized experiences, available on every plan, not just enterprise tiers.

So without wasting any time, let’s understand the flow of Shopify international ecommerce, how it actually works, and what to configure.
contentAfterToc:
How Shopify Markets Works

Shopify Markets lets you manage currency, language, domains, pricing, and duties per region, all from a single store admin. When a customer visits from France, they see euro pricing and French content; a customer from Japan sees yen and Japanese content, automatically, based on location. You’re running one store with multiple localized presentations, not maintaining separate storefronts for each country.

Setting Up Markets

In Shopify admin, go to Markets and add the countries or regions you want to sell into. You can group several countries into a regional market (like the EU) or set up single-country markets individually. For most growing brands, one primary market with regional submarkets is cleaner than many separate top-level markets; a US brand selling across Europe is usually better served by one EU market with country-level submarkets than four standalone ones.

Currencies

With Shopify Payments active, Shopify supports local currency display and checkout in over 130 currencies, converted automatically using live exchange rates. Displaying prices in a customer’s local currency measurably reduces cart abandonment for cross-border buyers; this isn’t a cosmetic feature; it directly affects conversion.

One common mistake: leaving live conversion on for highly volatile currency pairs, which can make pricing look inconsistent day-to-day. For your most important markets, consider setting fixed regional prices instead.

Localization

Language settings work per market, not per store, so you decide which languages each specific market sees. Translated storefronts with proper SEO structure matter here: search engines need to be able to crawl and index each localized version correctly, which ties directly into the domain strategy below.

Domains

You’ll need a custom domain (Shopify-managed or third-party) to set up international domains; your default myshopify.com domain can’t be used for this. Options include country-specific top-level domains, subdomains, or subfolders; for example, example.de for Germany or example.com/en-eu for a European market. Shopify handles hreflang tags automatically for subfolder-based markets; subdomain or separate-domain setups need manual verification. If you remove a market later, set up proper redirects so customers aren’t sent to broken pages.

Payments

Shopify Payments supports many local payment methods natively. Where it isn’t available, third-party gateways can fill the gap. A useful rule of thumb: if a payment method is used by more than 30% of consumers in a target market, it’s worth supporting directly; missing a dominant local payment preference is a real source of lost sales.

Operational Considerations

A few things catch stores off guard: inventory is shared across markets by default; a stockout in one market shows as out-of-stock everywhere unless you use shipping zones to scope availability. Duties and import taxes should be calculated and shown at checkout, not left as a surprise on delivery. And each market’s domain needs to be registered separately in Search Console, with its own submitted sitemap, for search visibility.

When You’ve Outgrown Standard Markets

Standard Markets handles the vast majority of international selling well. But once you’re managing complex multi-region operations at real scale, separate legal entities, deeply distinct catalogs per region, and high-volume enterprise logistics, that’s where Shopify Plus’s expanded market and expansion-store capacity starts to matter. Our guide on Shopify Plus for global brands covers what changes at that scale.

The Bottom Line

Shopify Markets makes international selling accessible without needing separate stores or enterprise-level infrastructure. Get currencies, domains, and localization configured correctly from the start, and the platform handles most of the complexity automatically.
